message.reasoning:
Let me evaluate each criterion.

C1 Introduction (10 marks): Mission, rationale, number of spacecraft, users. All addressed well: coral bleaching monitoring, GBR, one satellite justified, operator AIMS, customers GBRMPA, CSIRO, BoM. References [1]-[6]. Accomplished, high standard. Maybe 9. Some minor issues: reference [4] "Nature news article" vague; some claims. But strong. 9.

C2 Main body mission design (60 marks): Launch (Vega C, Kourou, comparison with Falcon 9, azimuth calc), orbit (SSO 600 km, elements, inclination calc, STK screenshots), manoeuvres (none, justified), ground station (Mount Pleasant, access report, 6 passes/day, data budget), duration/EOL (5 years, drag sail, decay calc). Screenshots STK, appendix file list. Very thorough. Issues: Vega C "has not yet flown, first flight planned 2021" – at time of 2020 report that is correct contextually. Launch vehicle choice rideshare to SSO – fine. Missing detailed link budget (acknowledged). Revisit calculation simplistic (2698 km spacing / 560 km ≈ 4.8 days, but ignores longitude convergence and roll constraints—actually spacing at equator 2698 km, but at 18° latitude spacing is 2698*cos(18°)=2567 km; minor). Area reachable with ±25° roll: 2×600×tan25 = 560 km total, that's correct as cross-track total swath ~560 km. But actually the ground track spacing at reef latitude ~2570 km; 2570/560 = 4.6 days, they say ~5, fine.

Data budget: 40,000 pixels/km² for 5 m GSD: 1/(5m)² = 40,000 per km². Yes. 60,000 km² × 40,000 × 4 bands × 12 bits = 1.152e11 bits = 115 Gbit. Correct. Compression 4:1 → 29 Gbit. Downlink 50 Mbit/s × 2000 s = 100 Gbit. Wait 34 minutes = 2040 s, ~2000 s → 100 Gbit. Correct. Margin 3.5. Good.

However, area imaged per day 60 km × 1000 km = 60,000 km² — a single strip of 1000 km along-track per day? At 7 km/s ground speed, 1000 km takes ~140 s; a pass over the reef can be much longer. Fine, plausible.

Orbit decay calc: Δa per orbit = 2π (C_D A/m) ρ a². Check: standard formula Δa = 2π (C_D A/m) ρ a² per orbit. With A=0.3, m=50, ρ=1e-13, a=6.978e6: (2.2*0.3/50)=0.0132; ρ a² = 1e-13 * 4.869e13 = 4.869; 2π*0.0132*4.869 = 0.404 m. Yes 0.40 m per orbit. Over 14.9 orbits/day × 365 = 5439 orbits/year → 0.40 × 5439 = 2176 m ≈ 2.2 km/yr. Consistent. Lifetime ≈ H/rate = 70/2.2 = 32 years. Good.

Sail: A=4.3: 0.4 × (4.3/0.3) = 5.73 m per orbit; ×5439 = 31.2 km/yr; 70/31 = 2.2 years. Consistent. Good.

Inclination calc: check cos i = -(dΩ/dt)/(1.5 J2 (R/a)² n). 1.5*1.0826e-3 = 1.6239e-3; (R/a)² = (6378/6978)² = 0.8354; n = 1.0831e-3. Product = 1.6239e-3*0.8354*1.0831e-3 = 1.469e-6. Hmm 1.6239e-3 × 0.8354 = 1.3567e-3; ×1.0831e-3 = 1.4694e-6. Then cos i = -1.991e-7/1.4694e-6 = -0.1355. Matches. Good.

Note SSO nodal rate required: 360°/365.25 days = 0.9856°/day = 1.991e-7 rad/s. Good.

Launch azimuth: sin β = cos i / cos φ = cos 97.79/cos 5.2. Magnitude 0.136, so β = -7.8° from north. Correct.

Spacecraft: aperture requirement 1.22 λ L / D; D = 1.22*0.5e-6*600e3/5 = 0.0732 m. Correct.

Period: T = 2π√(a³/μ) = 5801 s = 96.7 min. Correct.

Max pass duration 771 s hand calc: horizon-to-horizon at 600 km — geometric: central angle for horizon ~ (2*acos(R/(R+h))) = 2*acos(6378/6978)=2*24.0°=48.0°... Actually for a ground station at horizon, central angle = acos(R/(R+h)) = 24.0°, half-path central angle 24°, path angle 48°, time = 48/360 × 5801 = 773 s. Yes matches 771 s. Good. But passes over a ground station not at same latitude—maximum is over equator crossing geometry ~ similar. OK.

Small issue: "Vega C has not yet flown; first flight planned 2021" — consistent with 2020 report. Actually Vega C first flight was 2022. Fine.

Minor: "Spacing of ground tracks on one day (equator) 2π × 6,378 km × 5,801 s / 86,164 s" = 40074 × 0.06732 = 2698 km. Yes, correct (14.85 orbits/day → 15 gaps? 360/14.85 = 24.24° → 2698 km). Good. But dividing 2698 by 560 gives 4.8 days — but cross-track reach is ±280 km from track, so total 560; however adjacent track spacing at reef latitude ~2567 km; also, with 15 orbits per day each separated 24.24° in longitude, and the reef being 2000 km along-track... The revisit calculation is approximate but reasonable. Actually a more careful analysis: because adjacent tracks are 2698 km apart at the equator and each pass covers 60 km swath; the number of days to cover the reef at a given latitude with roll access ±280 km: tracks spaced ~2560 km, so 2560/560 ≈ 4.6 → 5 days. Fine.

The catch: descent node crossing 08:45 local time — fine.

Potential issue: "Access above 0° elevation" and then reducing to 10° elevation; reasonable.

Another potential issue: satellite mass 50 kg, 0.5×0.5×0.6 m, 0.3 m² cross-section — plausible.

Note: With X-band 50 Mbit/s, a 12 m antenna is large; they acknowledge power/link budget not computed. Fine.

So C2 is strong overall: Accomplished, 8-9. I'd give 9.

C3 Conclusion (10): Summarizes results with numbers, lists limitations. Accomplished 9.

C4 Presentation (20): Well-structured, executive summary, headings, labelled figures/tables, citations [1]-[15] all cited in text? Check [7] cited in launch, [8],[9],[10] in table, [11] inclination, [12] ground station, [13] Mount Pleasant, [14] IADC, [15] drag sail, [1]-[6] intro. All cited. Formatting: tables consistent, figures labelled. Minor issues: Figure 2 appears to lack axis... it's fine. Reference [4] "Nature, news article" – vague author, minor. Reference [15] Space Review article number only, vague. Overall high quality. Mark 8-9. Give 8.

R requirements check:
R1 yes; R2 yes; R3 yes; R4 yes; R5 yes; R6 yes; R7 yes; R8 yes; R9 yes (STK); R10 yes (screenshots + appendix listing files; files themselves presumably submitted in zip); R11 yes.

Technical issues list: no link budget (acknowledged); revisit/data budget approximations; Vega C statement about "not yet flown" now outdated but accurate at time; Figure 2 has no source/derivation given? It's likely from STK or MATLAB—not stated how generated; Table 5 access with 0° elevation requires terrain-free site, fine; reef coverage "one strip per day" with 60,000 km²/day is low—satellite could image much more; acknowledged? Not really. Also 45-day mosaic claim consistent.

Also note: "spacecraft is operated by AIMS through Mount Pleasant ground station in Tasmania" — Mount Pleasant is UTas-owned; they flag adding equipment. Fine.

Also the launch inclination: Kourou 5.2°N, azimuth 7.8° west of north — correct for retrograde SSO; but descending/ascending node definition: launching at azimuth measured from north positive east; -7.8° means 7.8° west of north. Correct.

One issue: Table 5 access durations with minimum 151 s at 0° elevation seems inconsistent — an access at 0° elevation with min duration 151 s is possible for a low pass. Fine.

Technical issue: statement "its depths have only been mapped to a resolution of 100 metres per pixel" – consistent with gbr100.

Overall marks: C1 9/10, C2 9/10, C3 9/10, C4 8/10.

Weighted: 0.1*9 + 0.6*9 + 0.1*9 + 0.2*8 = 0.9+5.4+0.9+1.6 = 8.8/10.
